passage: The campaign began with spearphishing emails that carried a weaponized Word document as an attachment.
Victims received a message urging them to click the link, which led to a fake login page used for credential harvesting.
The actors exploited a vulnerability in the company's internet-facing web server to obtain a foothold.
Operators logged in using stolen credentials obtained from an earlier breach.
The loader launched PowerShell with an encoded command to fetch the next stage.
A batch file was dropped and run through cmd.exe to copy the implant into place.
To remain on the system, the malware wrote a value under the Run key so it started at every logon.
The backdoor created a scheduled task using schtasks that executes every hour.
The group installed the payload as a new Windows service named to resemble a system component.
The shellcode was injected into explorer.exe to hide its activity from monitoring tools.
The configuration blob is base64 encoded and further XOR encoded to hinder static analysis.
The attackers dumped credentials from LSASS memory using a renamed copy of ProcDump.
A password spraying attack was run against exposed mail accounts over several days.
The implant records captured keystrokes and stores them in a local file.
It collects the computer name, OS version and installed patches and reports them to the server.
The tool runs tasklist to enumerate running processes and look for security products.
The intruders connected to servers over Remote Desktop to move laterally across the domain.
Files were copied to the admin shares of neighboring hosts and run with PsExec.
Documents of interest were compressed into a password protected RAR archive before leaving the network.
The malware takes screenshots every few minutes and saves them to disk.
Stolen data was uploaded to a Dropbox account controlled by the actors.
The ransomware encrypts files and drops a ransom note in every folder.
Before encryption, the operators ran vssadmin to remove shadow copies so victims could not restore files.
The sample uses certutil to download a second stage from a remote server.
Command and control traffic is wrapped in HTTPS POST requests to blend in with normal web traffic.
The malware queries domains produced by a domain generation algorithm to locate its server.
The operators disabled Windows Defender through a registry change before deploying the payload.
After execution the dropper removes itself from disk to hinder forensic analysis.
Employees opened the invoice attached to the email, which then silently launched a hidden script.
The attackers walked through the network looking for other computers they could reach.
The group abused a legitimate remote support tool already trusted in the environment to keep access.
Operators covered their tracks by erasing the Windows event logs on the compromised hosts.
The binary is named like a legitimate Windows utility and sits in a folder commonly used by the operating system.
The malware checks for signs of analysis tools and halts if it detects it is running inside a lab environment.
